newsitem.title: FRANCE: AGF profits jump 42 percent, hints at GAN bid.
newsitem.headline: AGF profits jump 42 percent, hints at GAN bid.

text.p: AGF , France's second largest insurer, reported on Thursday its 1996 profits jumped 42 percent and hinted it could bid for rival GAN to increase its clout following the Axa-UAP mega-merger.
Assurances Generales de France (AGF) said consolidated net profit rose to 1.54 billion francs ($269.3 million) from 1.08 billion on premium income that fell 10.4 percent to 69.35 billion francs.
On a like-for-like basis, stripping out changes in the group's structure, premium income rose 4.7 percent. The profits were in line with market expectations.

AGF chairman Antoine Jeancourt-Galignani said AGF, privatised last year, needed to know more about how the government would sell state-controlled Groupe des Assurances Nationales before saying it would bid for it.

"We are observing the situation...We have to know how, when and under what conditions it (the government) plans to privatise it," he said. But, he added, GAN had activities that "complement our own" and the government's pledge to cover its massive losses meant the insurer could look forward to a future as a "normal player" in the sector.
The government plans to pump 20 billion francs into GAN, hard hit by a property slump, to ready it for sale this year.
Jeancourt-Galignani said the merger announced late last year between French insurance heavyweights Axa and UAP had accelerated concentration in the sector and AGF could not "ignore events."
Analysts say AGF needs to build "critical mass" in the wake of the merger that created the world's second largest insurer.
At the same, referring to market speculation AGF could become a bid target, he warned any offer would be "hostile" as well as costly, in light of the sharp rise in AGF's share price.

"We do not consider a takeover to be in the interest of our shareholders," he said, adding AGF had not been informed of any stakebuilding in it. "We have a vocation to play the role of the second largest insurance group in France," he said. At the same time, he did not rule out alliances with other European groups.

AGF's shares, which closed up 1.90 percent at 214.50 francs on Thursday, have been buoyed by persistent rumours it could be subject of an offer from another European insurer as well as by its inclusion in the CAC-40 index of 40 leading shares.

There has been widespread market talk that German insurer Allianz might bid for AGF. Allianz said on Wednesday it wants to boost its French presence and was sizing up GAN but did not rule out an offer for AGF.

AGF said its 1996 profit jump was driven by a surge in earnings contributions from its insurance busineses, helped by an improvement in technical ratios. The increase was achieved despite a 14 percent fall in realisation of capital gains.
"We have had a 75 percent rise in net profits in two years," said Jeancourt-Galignani, adding AGF had largely dug itself out of the real estate woes that dogged it in the past.
Property lending arm, Comptoir des Entrepreneurs, which hemorrhaged red ink in the past, slashed its loss to 35 billion francs from a loss of 243 billion the previous year.

The earnings contribution from non-life insurance jumped 132 percent jump to 937 million francs. Life insurance kicked in 376 million francs, up 69.4 percent. Credit insurance contributed 341 million francs, up 27 percent.
But banking and financial services remained a weight, subtracting 526 million francs from profits compared with a drain of 490 million the previous year.

And the contribution from insurance outside France fell nearly 12 percent to 817 million, hit by a 273 million franc operating loss for British operations compared with an 81 million franc profit in 1995.
The British operations were hurt by a sharp deterioration in the domestic market and AGF hoped they would break even this year or at least show a "sharp improvement." ($ = 5.718 French Francs)
